Five unresolved, none wrong

📅 Oct 13, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The short version

  • When the document that would settle a question does not exist, estimate, label the estimate and say what would replace it.
  • Proportional allocation gives a tidy, constant rate that proves nothing about the loan. Pick a basis that follows how the thing really behaves.
  • Leave open items open. Five unresolved items are better than one wrong one.
  • A visible, reasoned estimate is a professional judgment. A silent one is a small misrepresentation.

There is a popular image of accounting as the discipline of exactness: every cent traced, every balance tied, nothing left to judgment. Practitioners know better. A surprising share of the work is deciding what to do when the document that would settle a question does not exist, cannot be obtained or arrives too late. How an accountant behaves in that gap says more about the quality of the books than any number of perfectly reconciled months.

Consider a common case. A growing company borrows from a revenue-based lender and, for most of a year, books each monthly repayment wholly against the loan balance. No interest is recorded. When someone notices, the lender’s statements for the later months are available, and the interest in them can be booked precisely. For four earlier months they are not. What is known is the total: the difference between what was paid and what the principal fell by comes to roughly $17,000. What is unknown is how that total divides between February, March, April and May.

How do you split interest you cannot see?

The easiest method is to allocate the total in proportion to the loan balance each month. It is quick, it ties to the known figure and it produces a pleasingly consistent result: an implied interest rate that is exactly the same in every month. People take that consistency as confirmation. A constant rate from proportional allocation says something about the method and nothing about the loan. The lender’s actual statements for the later months, as it happens, show rates that are far from constant.

My basis was days elapsed between payments, on the view that interest accrues with time. An unscheduled wire counted as a payment on its own date, and a refund counted from its own date. The monthly figures came out uneven, less elegant and more defensible. If the loan terms say interest works differently, the basis changes, and that is one more reason to write the basis down. Both methods are estimates. Only one is built on the mechanics of the thing being estimated.

Why should the memo say it is an estimate?

The choice of method matters less than what is written beside it. The journal entries in this case carry memos stating that the figures are an estimate reconstructed from payment history and not taken from lender statements, describing the basis, and noting that they will be replaced if the statements turn up. A reader who opens the ledger in three years, an auditor or a buyer’s adviser, can see at once which numbers are evidenced and which are judged.

The same habit shows up elsewhere in my work. When four months of credit-card statements could not be obtained from an issuer, I reconciled the account across the gap to a balance derived from the surrounding statements, and the working paper says that this was done and why. When a run of equipment purchases had been posted to a fixed-asset account, I raised whether they should have been capitalized as a policy question for the client and did not correct it as an error. Until someone with authority decides, consistency of treatment governs. When a check could not be settled, I left it open and labeled it as open. My working rule: better five unresolved items than one wrong one.

Why is it so hard to leave items open?

The incentives point the other way. A reconciliation that closes at zero looks like competence. A working paper with open items looks unfinished. The accounting packages I use reinforce the bias by offering, at the end of every reconciliation, to post any remaining difference automatically, with no explanation required. Multiplied across thousands of small businesses, the result is a large volume of books that balance perfectly and cannot be relied on.

What works against that is mostly procedure:

  • Investigate before adjusting. A difference is a clue. Bisect the period, find the item, fix it where it lives. (The search problems in “The search that found nothing” are a good reason to do this carefully.)
  • Set a threshold for stopping. Above a stated amount, an unexplained difference halts the work and goes to someone with authority instead of into an adjusting entry.
  • Write memos that answer questions before they are asked. The amount, the period, what was tested, what was ruled out, the probable cause and what would resolve it.
  • Say what the working paper did not test. Limitations stated plainly protect the reader, and you.

Corrections go in as new entries and never as edits, so the error and its fix both stay visible. “The customer who wasn’t there” shows what that looks like over a full year.

What does a good estimate look like to the reader?

Owners, lenders, investors and tax authorities do not expect perfection. They expect that the people preparing the numbers know which ones are firm and which are soft, and will say so. An estimate that is disclosed, reasoned and replaceable is a professional judgment. The same estimate posted silently as if it were a fact is a small misrepresentation, however close to the truth it turns out to be.

The habit of mind is easy to state and hard to keep. When you do not know, say so, show your working, and leave the door open for the evidence to arrive. Books kept that way will sometimes look messier than their neighbors’. They will also be the ones still standing when somebody checks.

This is my own practice and not formal accounting guidance. Which treatment applies to a given estimate depends on the facts and the framework your books follow, so confirm it with your accountant or auditor.

The search that found nothing

📅 Oct 13, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The short version

  • An empty search result is not a fact until you have shown the search can find something.
  • Run the same search for an item you know exists, close in date and amount, before you believe a “no such transaction.”
  • Extracted data has to foot back to the source’s own totals before you use it.
  • Two identical charges on the same day are often two real charges. Count rendered rows, not a deduplicated set.

In a biology lab, a careful researcher does not report a negative result without a positive control. If a test for a protein comes back empty, the first question is whether the test would have detected the protein had it been there. So alongside the real sample runs a second one known to contain it. If the control lights up and the sample does not, the negative means something. If neither lights up, the experiment has measured nothing except its own failure.

Accounting has no equivalent habit, and it needs one. Much of modern bookkeeping consists of asking software questions and believing the answers. Is there a payment of $368 in March? Search returns nothing. Has this transaction been edited since it was reconciled? The audit log for the period is empty. Are there any deposits from this processor after May? The filtered register shows none. Each empty result gets treated as a fact. Very often it is a filter that did not work.

How often does accounting software return nothing by mistake?

Over a single reconciliation engagement this year I kept a tally of the times a search or filter in a widely used accounting package returned nothing when the thing I wanted was there. There were eight. Among them: a search box that matched only when the amount was typed with a dollar sign. A register date filter that silently ignored the range I entered. An audit log whose custom date range returned nothing at all. A reconciliation screen that loaded transactions lazily and stopped at 150 rows, so the 151st, however clearly present, could not be found by scrolling.

None of these is a scandal. Every piece of software has quirks. The danger is in the asymmetry of the results. A filter that wrongly returns something gets noticed immediately, because the something is visibly wrong. A filter that wrongly returns nothing looks exactly like the truth. In a reconciliation, “no such transaction” leads straight to a conclusion: the item is missing, post it. Post it on the strength of a broken filter and the item is now in the books twice.

The remedy is cheap. Before believing a search that returns nothing, run the same search for something known to exist, ideally something similar in date and amount. If that comes back, the empty result has earned some credibility. If it does not, the tool is what needs investigating, not the ledger.

What happens when a script drops the decimal?

The same logic applies to the code accountants increasingly write themselves. A short script that extracts transaction lines from a stack of credit-card statements is reasonable automation. It turns a day of typing into a minute of processing. One such script, run on four months of statements, reconciled to the penny in two months and missed by a cent in one and by exactly a dollar in another.

The cause was a pattern that expected at least one digit before the decimal point. The card issuer printed amounts under a dollar as “.01” and “.99”, with no leading zero, so every sub-dollar charge was invisible to the extraction. The books were right. The extracted data was wrong, and the script reported it with complete confidence. The fix took a minute. Finding the problem took the habit of footing the extracted lines back to the statement’s own printed totals before using them for anything.

When are duplicate transactions real?

The instinct to clean data can be as dangerous as the failure to check it. Analysts are trained to deduplicate. In transaction data, though, two charges on the same card, on the same day, for the same amount, from the same merchant are frequently two genuine charges. A car-sharing account in one engagement produced thirteen such pairs in four months. Deduplicating them would have deleted real expenses and created a reconciliation difference nobody could explain.

My working rule is to count rendered rows, as they appear in the source, and never a deduplicated set. Where two lines look identical, match them one-to-one against an independent record, such as the card statement, instead of collapsing them.

A short field guide

For finance teams doing more of their own data work, four habits matter:

  • Give an empty result a positive control before you believe it.
  • Foot extracted data back to the source’s own totals before you use it.
  • Count what is rendered, not what survives deduplication.
  • Read a report’s full output rather than what fits on the screen, and check that a running balance lands on the stated total.

Fraud examiners will recognize the principle underneath. Absence of evidence is evidence of absence only when the search could have found the evidence. An accountant who analyzes data without that rule is asking the software for reassurance, and the software is always happy to oblige.

The predictable business with unpredictable books

📅 Oct 13, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The short version

  • Most MSPs run three businesses through one revenue line, and the blended gross margin describes none of them.
  • Agreements bill in advance and licenses bill in arrears, so a month’s margin is partly fiction until cost and revenue are matched by agreement.
  • A monthly match of cost to revenue by agreement, product and sales order catches more leakage than a variance report.
  • Sales tax on managed services depends on the state. Someone has to own that calendar.

The pitch of a managed service provider (MSP) is reassuringly dull. For a fixed monthly fee per user or per device, it will keep a firm’s laptops patched, its servers backed up and its email out of the hands of fraudsters. Clients like the predictability. Buyers like it too, and in the deals I have seen they pay for recurring revenue.

Open the books of a typical small or mid-sized provider, though, and predictability is in short supply. Revenue lands in the wrong month. Costs arrive a month late. Hardware resale swells the top line and flatters growth while doing little for profit. Ask the owner what the gross margin is on managed services, separate from everything else, and the honest answer is often a shrug.

The cause is the business model. It has three features that ordinary small-business accounting handles poorly.

Why does a blended gross margin mislead?

Most MSPs I have worked with are really three businesses sharing a bank account. There is the recurring service, which is high-margin and labor-intensive. There is resale of third-party licenses, such as Microsoft 365 or security software, which is low-margin and almost entirely cost of goods. And there is project and hardware work, which is lumpy and moves cash in large chunks. Lumped into a single revenue line, the three produce a gross margin that describes none of them.

An illustrative month for a provider with roughly $250,000 in monthly billings shows how much the blend can hide:

Revenue stream (illustrative)RevenueDirect costGross marginManaged services (agreements)$140,000$56,00060%License resale$60,000$51,00015%Hardware and projects$50,000$40,00020%Blended$250,000$147,00041%

These figures are made up to show the mechanics. They are not benchmarks.

A blended 41% looks respectable. It also hides that a quarter of the revenue earns 15%, and that a month with a large hardware order will push the headline margin down even though the core business has not changed at all. Owners who manage to the blended figure end up chasing the wrong problems.

Why does the monthly close drift?

Timing. In the setups I have seen, agreements are billed in advance, on the first of the month, through a professional services automation (PSA) platform such as ConnectWise. Licensing suppliers, especially distributors, tend to bill in arrears for consumption already incurred. So January’s revenue sits beside December’s license costs, and any month in which seat counts change produces a gross-margin figure that is partly fiction.

The PSA adds to the difficulty. In the ConnectWise-to-QuickBooks setups I have worked with, a recurring agreement, its mid-month additions, a one-off sales order and the procurement of the hardware behind it are separate objects, each with its own dates and billing status. When they sync into QuickBooks, they arrive as invoices dated when they were generated, not when the service was delivered. An invoice for a prorated addition in late March can be dated April 2. A sales order invoiced in installments can carry a date that matches neither the order nor the shipment. Month-end close at an MSP is, to a surprising degree, the work of putting each invoice back in the period it belongs to and finding the cost that goes with it.

My fix is to match cost to revenue at the level where they are actually linked: the agreement, the product and the sales order, not the account. Where revenue for a product exists without its cost, or cost without revenue, there is either an unbilled service or an unrecorded bill. Run monthly, this one exercise has caught more leakage in my clients’ books than any number of variance analyses on the profit and loss account.

Which taxes catch MSPs out?

Managed IT services sit in a gray zone of American sales-tax law. In my experience some states tax software and digital services, some tax certain IT services, and many treat a bundle of taxable and non-taxable elements by rules that differ in detail from one statehouse to the next. Picture a provider in one state with clients in two others. It can face three different answers to the question of what is taxable in a monthly agreement that includes licenses, monitoring and help-desk time.

Getting this wrong is expensive in a particular way. Sales tax that was never collected from customers is still owed by the provider, and it is hard to recover from clients years later. Payroll taxes add their own traps. I have seen state unemployment registrations lapse, quarterly returns go unfiled during a change of payroll provider, and a small penalty notice turn into a lien. None of this is exotic. It is small administrative facts that nobody owns.

Sales-tax and payroll rules vary by state and change over time, and this article is not tax advice. Check your own situation with a tax professional who knows your states.

Where does the money hide?

Some sector-specific wrinkles. The account-manager commissions I have seen are often calculated on revenue rather than margin, which rewards selling low-margin licenses. Some providers serve schools and libraries funded through the federal E-rate program, where payment depends on paperwork filed with a third party. Receivables there can sit open for months for reasons that have nothing to do with the client’s willingness to pay.

The common thread is that the information needed to run an MSP well already exists, scattered across the PSA, the distributor portals, the payroll system and the accounting software. What is usually missing is the connective tissue: a chart of accounts that separates the three businesses, a close process that dates revenue by service period, a monthly match of cost to revenue by agreement, and someone responsible for the tax calendar.

Nobody has to buy new software for this. The provider has to keep its own books with the discipline it promises for its clients’ servers. Most MSPs would never tolerate a backup that had not been tested. A margin that has not been tested is the same sort of risk.

Nothing failed. Everything was wrong

📅 Oct 12, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The short version

  • A green tick or a “sync completed” line says the connection is alive. It says nothing about whether the data that travelled was complete or right.
  • Silent faults come in five families: records that never arrive, arrive twice, arrive altered, land in the wrong account, or lose their state, such as a reconciled flag.
  • Bank rules fail quietly too: a rule that was edited, or wrong from the start, can misfile the same payee for months.
  • A reconciliation shows that the book agrees with the bank at one moment. It does not show that the book agrees with the source system.
  • Count and total on both sides of every integration, by day and by account, and treat edits by “System” as a finding.

Every finance team has a dashboard light that reassures it. In the accounting software it is usually a small green tick beside the bank feed, or a line in the integration log that says “sync completed”. The tick means the connection is alive. It says nothing about whether what travelled down the connection was complete, correct or even the right thing.

That distinction sounds pedantic until it costs money. The cases in this piece come from my own work and from other controllers I have worked with. Take one from earlier this year: a mid-sized American services company found that its bank feed had stopped delivering one category of deposit, the daily settlements from its card processor, from one Tuesday in May. The feed did not disconnect. It went on delivering payroll debits, card payments and transfers on schedule, and the green tick stayed green. Only the settlements vanished. By the time anyone looked, a dozen deposits worth well over $100,000 were missing from the books, and a second settlement channel turned out to have failed in the same way. When the provider later repaired a genuine disconnection, the error code it fixed had nothing to do with the gap.

Nobody had done anything wrong. That is the problem.

A taxonomy of quiet

Engineers have a name for this class of fault: silent data corruption. Data is altered, dropped or duplicated somewhere between source and destination without any component raising an alarm. In storage systems it is treated as a serious hazard and hunted with checksums. In accounting, where the stakes are arguably higher, it is mostly hunted by luck and by the month-end close.

The faults fall into a handful of recognizable families:

  • A record exists in the source system and never arrives. The missing settlements above are the textbook case.
  • A record arrives twice, often because a retry succeeded after a timeout that was logged as a failure.
  • A record arrives with a field changed: a date shifted to the posting day rather than the service day, a customer reassigned to a default, an amount rounded.
  • The record is right but lands in the wrong account, usually because an automated rule has been edited, or was wrong from the start.
  • State loss. Something that was true about a record stops being true. A reconciled transaction quietly loses its reconciled status.

The last family is the strangest, and the least discussed. In the same company, the audit trail on one ordinary deposit showed thirteen edits over two days, each attributed not to a person but to “System”, each toggling the transaction between cleared and not cleared. Every bank transaction after a certain date had lost its reconciliation flag. The software’s own reports described the affected entries as “deleted” with a current amount of zero, although they were plainly intact. Anyone reading that report cold would conclude that money had been removed from the books.

The rule that changed

Misclassification deserves particular attention, because modern bookkeeping runs on rules. A mid-market company may have several hundred bank rules, each telling the software that a payee or a description belongs to a particular account. Rules are efficient and invisible, which is a dangerous combination.

In the case above, one rule had posted a payroll provider’s monthly fee correctly to payroll expense for four months, then began posting it somewhere else. Nobody remembered changing it. A second rule pointed at the same wrong account. A third had been sending the employer’s pension match into a liability account, where it accumulated for three months to just over $12,000 before anyone noticed that a balance which should be zero was not. Individually each amount was small. Together they distorted payroll cost, inflated a liability and nudged three months of management accounts in the wrong direction.

I have seen the same pattern wherever an operational platform feeds the ledger. A professional-services automation (PSA) tool such as ConnectWise has synced invoices into QuickBooks perfectly well while carrying the invoice date rather than the service period, so that a month’s recurring revenue straddled two periods in the books. A dealership management system has pushed a day’s sales as a summary, and when one day failed to post, the summary for the next day looked entirely normal. The integration is not broken. It is simply doing something slightly different from what the accountant assumes.

Why the close does not catch it

The conventional defense is the bank reconciliation, and it is a good one. But it has blind spots. A reconciliation proves that the book agrees with the bank at a moment in time. It does not prove that the book agrees with the source system that generated the revenue, nor that the transactions are in the right accounts, nor that last month’s reconciliation is still intact this month. A dropped deposit shows up as a reconciliation difference only if someone reconciles; on accounts nobody has reconciled for a year, the error simply compounds.

There is also a human pattern. When a reconciliation is out by a few hundred dollars, the path of least resistance is an adjusting entry. Software makes this easy: several of the products I have worked with will offer to post the difference automatically. Each such entry converts a symptom of corruption into a permanent, unexplained line in the ledger. Do that for a year and the books balance perfectly, and explain nothing.

Checksums for the ledger

The remedy borrows from the engineers. Rather than trusting that a sync succeeded, one counts and totals independently on both sides of the integration and compares the results, by day, by account and by customer. If the processor says 474 payments settled on a given day and the ledger holds 474 lines summing to the same figure, the batch is probably intact. If it holds 473, or the right count with the wrong total, something has drifted, and the comparison says where to look.

This is the idea behind LedgerDrift, an open-source toolkit I have been developing for some two years and am now piloting with several organizations, from a vehicle dealership to a legal services firm. It does not replace the close. It runs alongside the integration, fingerprints what leaves the source system and what lands in the ledger, and reports the differences in terms an accountant can act on: missing, duplicated, altered, misfiled, or no longer reconciled.

The principle matters more than the tool. Any finance team can apply it with a spreadsheet and some discipline: never accept a sync log as evidence; reconcile counts as well as amounts; check that the rules engine still says what it said last quarter; and treat an audit trail full of edits by “System” as a finding rather than a curiosity.

The green tick will go on glowing. It was only ever telling you that the pipe was connected, never what came out of it.

Small Business Security Setup: What I Use Every Day

📅 Oct 12, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The short version

  • I run most of my day on Proton’s tools and a few privacy-first apps, all on personal plans.
  • For a small team I would start with two things: a shared password vault with generated passwords, and aliases on a company-owned address.
  • Physical security keys come second, only for the accounts that matter most.
  • I have not tested these tools inside a company, so what I say about teams is a recommendation.

This is the security setup I run every day, and the starting point I would give a small business.

Most of my working day runs on a handful of tools, and I picked them for one reason: I want to know who can see my data. Some come from Proton. Some are small apps I found while looking for a way out of Google. I pay for Proton’s Duo plan, billed yearly, and for most of the other tools on personal plans. I have never tested any of them inside a company. So this article has two parts. First, what I use and why. Then the order I would give a business of five people, which is a recommendation and not a report.

How long did it take to leave Gmail and Hotmail?

About a month and a half, maybe two. I had been using the internet hard for years, so I had accounts everywhere. My rule was simple. Every time an email landed in my Gmail or Hotmail, I went to the site that sent it and changed my registered address to an alias. All the aliases forward to my Proton mailbox.

A couple of years later I still do it, but now about once every six months, because almost nothing arrives at the old addresses. Everything comes through the aliases.

The part that dragged was the sites that would not let me change my email. For those I had to write to support and ask them to change it by hand, or open a new account. That was the most tiresome step of the whole move. The rest has worked very well. The alias setup has its own article: Email Aliases: Why I Use a Different Address for Every Site.

What runs on my computer all day?

The VPN is on from the moment I turn the computer on until I shut it down. It starts by itself. I stopped noticing the change in speed a while ago. Now and then it hangs, which happens with any VPN, and I disconnect and reconnect. It lands on a faster server and that is the end of it.

Proton Mail is where everything arrives. Proton Calendar holds my whole day, and I like not having to wonder whether my schedule is feeding somebody’s AI model.

Proton Drive is the one I lean on most. It holds a copy of my entire computer, so I can reach my files from anywhere, even when I am away from home and need one specific file. I also send heavy files through it. It works well, and it is good to look at.

How I set it up is the useful part. I keep everything in one single folder. Inside it there are thousands of subfolders, but from the outside it is one folder, and that is the only thing I upload. If you want an easy backup, do the same: pick the one folder that holds everything vital, copy it to an external drive, and put it in your cloud. You only have to look after that one.

Proton Pass is my backup password manager. Bitwarden is the main one. Why I keep two is in Why I Keep My Passwords in Two Password Managers.

How do I use AI with sensitive files?

Proton has its own assistant, Lumo. Proton says it does not use your conversations to train the model, and it protects your data. That is the reason I use it for sensitive material, such as analyzing PDFs that carry private information. It keeps getting better, with something new added every few months.

Which Proton tools do I skip?

Proton Docs and Proton Sheets. They still feel like they need more development, so I don’t use them.

Proton Wallet is a Bitcoin wallet. I know how it works and I have looked at it, but I have never used it.

I have never used Proton Meet. As of October 2026, my Duo plan gives me the same limits as the free tier: up to 5 new meeting links a day, 50 people per meeting, calls of 60 minutes and one active meeting at a time. It looks good on paper. I have only read about it, so I won’t pretend to review it.

Why did I leave Google Photos?

I already had Google Photos. Then I started thinking about how much of my life was sitting there, and about a company that trains AI models having access to all of it. That bothered me. I downloaded Ente Photos and paid for the yearly plan.

It does what Google Photos did for me. Ente says its face recognition runs on the device. I can’t check that myself, so I’m repeating what its policies say. It is fast, and it syncs across all my devices. The AI extras are gone, and I don’t miss them.

For notes I use Notesnook. My drafts, my notes and my plans all live there, and I like how it works. The free plan is good enough that I would tell anyone to start with it. I tried Notion and never really understood it.

Where does a small business security setup start?

I have no company-plan numbers for any of these tools. I have not priced them, so I won’t give a monthly figure. I also know that sharing a vault on a personal plan has limits, and I haven’t checked what they are. What I can give you is the order I would follow.

First, the passwords. Put every password the team shares into a shared Bitwarden vault, open only to the people who need it. Nobody makes up a password by hand. The manager generates it, at least 20 characters if you can, and never fewer than 15. For myself I go to 24 or more.

Then add the secret ending I described in the password article, the short piece that never goes into the vault. With so few people you can agree on it together, and if one person forgets it, another can help. If someone leaves the team, change the ending. It is a lot of work. It is worth it.

When you need to pass a text or a file, use Bitwarden Send. It is an option inside the app, I use it often, and it beats WhatsApp.

Second, aliases. Sign up for services with an address that belongs to the company, not necessarily the official one. That keeps the company’s main address from being attached to every site and tool somebody tries out. If one starts sending spam or turns out to have leaked data, you switch that alias off. The how-to is in the alias article.

Those two, in that order. Everything else comes after.

Is any of this too much?

No. I don’t think any of it is excessive, for a company or for a person. It is the minimum anyone should have today.

Some people will call it too much work. A few might even call it paranoia. I enjoy it. It has been a fun process, and it is useful. People who could have laughed at it have been hacked since, and they ended up agreeing with me.

There is a second level: physical security keys. I have two. One is my main key, which I carry with me, and the other is the spare. Both are registered on the same sites. Every time I sign up for a site with a key, I register the second one right then, so that if I lose the first I still get in with the other. If a site allows a third, I create it in Bitwarden, and that works.

I also use passkeys saved in Bitwarden, and I use them all the time. On one platform I log into for work, I get in with a passkey. Some services are already removing the password altogether. We are heading toward a world with fewer passwords and more passkeys.

Keys are for accounts that need far more protection, like the ones that hold money or the company’s main systems. A key works together with the password. I would not put one on everything, only where the extra trouble pays off.

This is my experience, not security advice. Features and plans change, so check each provider.

📅 Oct 09, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Insurance Adviser recently interviewed this year’s Broker of the Year award state winners, we’ve reproduced their interview with our own Shannan Gardner so our clients and other partners can hear what makes Shannan a standout in this year’s awards.

If you’d prefer to read the full article please click through here.

‘The role of a broker will be different in the next decade than what it is today.’ Do you agree/disagree with this statement?

I strongly agree. I have already seen a significant shift in broking from when I first started in the industry. Back then, we were manually printing closings, putting them into pigeonholes, and packaging them up to be posted on a Friday afternoon. Technology, AI and automation will continue to remove a lot of the administrative heavy lifting from the broker’s day-to-day role. Routine processing, data entry, and parts of placement may become faster and more streamlined. But I do not believe that makes brokers less relevant. In fact, I think it makes our advisory role even more important.

The future broker will be less transactional and more educational for clients. Clients will need us to help them navigate an increasingly complex risk environment, interpret information and make confident decisions. Our value will come from our technical knowledge, but also from our ability to provide empathy, negotiate creatively and advocate strongly. The broker of the future will need to be tech empowered, but still deeply human. We need to embrace innovation while maintaining the personable, relationship-driven approach that sits at the heart of good broking.

What is your broking philosophy?

My broking philosophy is simple: put the client’s interests at the centre of every decision and build trusted relationships that last well beyond the renewal date. I believe our role extends far beyond arranging insurance. It is about deeply understanding a client’s business and helping them protect their assets as if they were my own.

A strong broker should not just know the policy wording; they should understand the client’s operations, pressures, exposures and long-term goals. A major part of my approach involves stripping away industry jargon. I want to ensure my clients are fully aware of exactly what they are covered for, and just as importantly, what they are not covered for, so there are no surprises at claim time.

Ultimately, I pride myself on the integrity I’ve built over the years – being open, honest and transparent with clients, underwriters and key partners, which, to me, are the defining features of a great broker.

What is the most important emerging risk the profession needs to be ready for?

Cyber risk remains a major issue, but I believe the broader challenge is business resilience in an increasingly uncertain world. Businesses are now facing threats that span climate-related events, supply chain disruption, workforce shortages, inflationary pressures and rapid technological change, which can all combine to create significant operational and financial stress. For many clients, a single event can have a ripple effect across their entire business.

As brokers, we need to move beyond generic insurance placement conversations and help clients think more broadly about resilience. That means talking about risk management, business continuity plans, crisis preparedness, contractual exposures, and the limitations of insurance solutions. Insurance will always be a critical part of the discussion, but it cannot be the only part. Our profession has an opportunity to help clients prepare for disruption before it happens, not just support them after a loss occurs.

Brokers who can bridge the gap between risk management and insurance advice will play an increasingly important role in helping businesses remain strong, adaptable and prepared.

Insurance broking is facing a challenge when it comes to addressing the knowledge and skills gap. What are your thoughts on this?

The knowledge and skills gap is one of the most important challenges facing our industry. Insurance has been an incredibly rewarding profession for me, but many young people simply do not know it exists as a career path. At the same time, we are seeing many experienced brokers retire, which means the industry is at risk of losing decades of technical knowledge.

I don’t believe the answer is recruitment alone. We need to invest in development. That means creating structured pathways that combine technical learning, practical experience and mentoring. Broking is not a profession you learn from a textbook alone.

You build confidence and judgement over time by working with clients, learning from experienced brokers, and understanding how advice works in real situations.

Programs such as the NIBA Mentoring Program, career expos that showcase the industry, and experienced brokers willing to step up and share their knowledge are all important. If we invest properly in the next generation, we can close the skills gap and ensure insurance broking remains a credible, respected and future-ready profession.

If you were to be crowned the national Broker of the Year winner, what would that recognition mean to you?

I have thought a lot about this since winning the SA/NT award, and it would be such an incredible honour. For me, it would not be about the title itself. It would be about what that recognition represents. It would recognise the clients who have trusted me with their businesses, the colleagues and mentors who have supported my development, and the strong relationships

I have built with insurers and industry partners over the past two decades. It would also reflect the values that I hold close to my heart: integrity, professionalism and a genuine commitment to helping others, not only within the insurance industry but through my volunteer work with the SA State Emergency Service.

To be recognised nationally would be incredibly meaningful because it would reflect not just one achievement, but years of dedication to the profession. Most importantly, I would see the recognition as motivation to keep raising standards, supporting the next generation of brokers, and advocating for the value our profession brings to clients, businesses and communities every day.

The post SPOTLIGHT / 2026 SA/NT Broker of the Year Award Winner appeared first on Guardian Insurance Brokers.

Wie sichtbar ist deine Marke in ChatGPT und Microsoft Copilot? Welche Chancen bieten digitale Zwillinge für die Marktforschung? Und wie gelingt vertrauenswürdige Kommunikation im KI-Zeitalter? Diese und weitere Zukunftsfragen standen im Mittelpunkt des 4. PR Tech Day von »OBSERVER« und den CommClubs Bayern.

Am 6. Oktober 2026 diskutierten Expert:innen von Microsoft, Edelman, FINN Partners, LOBECO und weiteren Unternehmen im Presseclub Nürnberg über die neuesten KI-Trends und ihre konkreten Auswirkungen auf PR, Marketing und Unternehmenskommunikation.

Der 4. PR Tech Day brachte Kommunikationsprofis, Marketingverantwortliche und Branchenexpert:innen sowohl vor Ort als auch online zusammen. Nach der Begrüßung durch Florian Freiherr von Hornstein, Präsident der CommClubs Bayern, boten neun Fachvorträge und eine abschließende Paneldiskussion spannende Einblicke in die digitale Transformation der Kommunikationsbranche.

Die zentrale Botschaft des Nachmittags: Künstliche Intelligenz verändert nicht nur, wie wir kommunizieren, sondern auch, wie Informationen gefunden, Marken wahrgenommen und Vertrauen aufgebaut werden. Für Unternehmen und PR-Agenturen entstehen dadurch neue Herausforderungen, aber auch enorme Chancen.

Von SEO zu GEO: Warum KI-Sichtbarkeit für Unternehmen immer wichtiger wird

Wer heute nach Produkten, Dienstleistungen oder Unternehmen sucht, nutzt längst nicht mehr ausschließlich klassische Suchmaschinen. Generative KI-Systeme wie ChatGPT und Microsoft Copilot entwickeln sich zunehmend zu wichtigen Informationsquellen.

Damit rückt ein neues Thema in den Fokus der strategischen Unternehmenskommunikation: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO).

Während Search Engine Optimization (SEO) darauf abzielt, Websites in klassischen Suchergebnissen möglichst gut zu positionieren, beschäftigt sich GEO mit der Sichtbarkeit von Marken, Unternehmen und Produkten in KI-generierten Antworten.

Anton Bühl, Geschäftsleiter Digital bei PER Connect, verdeutlichte anhand eines konkreten Unternehmensbeispiels, wie Large Language Models (LLMs) zu einem eigenständigen Kommunikationskanal werden.

Für Kommunikationsverantwortliche ergeben sich daraus entscheidende Fragen: Wird die eigene Marke in relevanten KI-Antworten überhaupt erwähnt? Welche Informationen geben KI-Systeme über das Unternehmen aus? Und wie lässt sich die digitale Präsenz gezielt verbessern?

Prompt Monitoring: Die neue Dimension der Medienbeobachtung

Wie Unternehmen ihre KI-Sichtbarkeit systematisch analysieren können, zeigte Stephan Ifkovits, Head of Communications & Marketing bei »OBSERVER«.

Sein Vortrag machte deutlich, dass modernes Brand Monitoring nicht mehr bei klassischen Medien, Online-Nachrichten und Social Media endet. Auch die Antworten generativer KI-Systeme werden für das Reputationsmanagement zunehmend relevant.

Mit Prompt Monitoring entsteht eine zusätzliche Disziplin der Medienbeobachtung. Dabei werden gezielte Fragen an KI-Systeme gestellt und die generierten Antworten regelmäßig analysiert. So lässt sich nachvollziehen, ob und in welchem Zusammenhang eine Marke erwähnt wird und wie sich ihre Darstellung im Zeitverlauf verändert.

Ifkovits gab praxisnahe Einblicke in relevante Prompt-Kategorien, geeignete Monitoring-Intervalle und Möglichkeiten zur Auswertung der Ergebnisse.

„Die Antworten von ChatGPT, Copilot und anderen KI-Systemen prägen zunehmend das Markenbild. Mit dem Prompt Monitoring schaffen wir die Grundlage, um diese neue Form der Sichtbarkeit zu beobachten und liefern so ein wichtiges Instrument für das eigene Reputationsmanagement.“

— Stephan Ifkovits, »OBSERVER«

Für PR- und Marketingteams bedeutet das: Wer seine Markenreputation umfassend verstehen möchte, sollte künftig auch berücksichtigen, welches Bild generative KI-Systeme vom eigenen Unternehmen vermitteln.

Vertrauen im KI-Zeitalter: Warum Glaubwürdigkeit wichtiger denn je ist

KI ermöglicht es Unternehmen, Inhalte schneller zu produzieren, Kommunikationsprozesse zu automatisieren und Zielgruppen effizienter anzusprechen. Doch mit den technologischen Möglichkeiten wächst auch die Bedeutung eines entscheidenden Erfolgsfaktors: Vertrauen.

Nils Giese, CEO von Edelman Germany, widmete sich der Frage, wie Unternehmen in einer zunehmend KI-geprägten Informationslandschaft glaubwürdig bleiben.

Seine zentrale Botschaft: Reichweite und Aufmerksamkeit allein reichen nicht aus, um langfristig erfolgreiche Kommunikation zu gestalten. Entscheidend sind vertrauensvolle Beziehungen zu den eigenen Zielgruppen.

Gerade in einer AI-first-Welt, in der Inhalte automatisiert erstellt und verbreitet werden können, gewinnen Authentizität, Transparenz und nachvollziehbare Informationen an Bedeutung.

KI in der PR: Effizienz steigern, Authentizität bewahren

Wie sich Künstliche Intelligenz produktiv in die Kommunikationsarbeit integrieren lässt, beleuchteten Gerrit Gericke, Managing Director Technology bei Edelman, und André Pechmann, Director Communications bei Microsoft.

Ob Pressemitteilungen, Reden, Gastbeiträge oder Social-Media-Posts: Generative KI kann PR-Teams bei zahlreichen Aufgaben unterstützen und zeitaufwendige Arbeitsschritte beschleunigen. Doch die Geschwindigkeit der Content-Produktion darf nicht zulasten der Qualität gehen.

Die Herausforderung besteht darin, KI als leistungsfähiges Werkzeug einzusetzen, ohne die menschliche Verantwortung für Inhalte, Botschaften und strategische Entscheidungen abzugeben.

Für Kommunikationsabteilungen bedeutet das, klare Qualitätsstandards zu definieren, KI-generierte Inhalte kritisch zu prüfen und Transparenz dort sicherzustellen, wo sie erforderlich ist.

Digitale Zwillinge: Neue Perspektiven für Markt- und Meinungsforschung

Während viele Unternehmen KI vor allem mit Textgenerierung, Bildbearbeitung oder Automatisierung verbinden, eröffnen sich auch in der Markt- und Meinungsforschung neue Anwendungsmöglichkeiten.

Florian Laszlo, CEO von »OBSERVER«, zeigte in seinem Vortrag, welches Potenzial digitale Zwillinge für die Analyse gesellschaftlicher Zielgruppen bieten.

Digitale Zwillinge sind virtuelle Modelle, die auf umfangreichen Datenbeständen basieren und bestimmte Eigenschaften oder Verhaltensweisen realer Systeme beziehungsweise Bevölkerungsgruppen simulieren können.

In der Industrie wird diese Technologie bereits seit Jahren eingesetzt. Nun entstehen auch für Marketing, Kommunikation und Sozialwissenschaften neue Perspektiven.

Wie können digitale Zwillinge die Marktforschung unterstützen?

Klassische Befragungen stehen zunehmend vor Herausforderungen: Die Teilnahmebereitschaft sinkt, die Erhebungskosten steigen und bestimmte Zielgruppen sind nur schwer erreichbar.

KI-gestützte Bevölkerungsmodelle könnten hier künftig ergänzende Analysemöglichkeiten schaffen. Durch die intelligente Verknüpfung unterschiedlicher Datenquellen lassen sich virtuelle Zielgruppen entwickeln, mit denen bestimmte Fragestellungen und Szenarien simuliert werden können.

Besonders für die B2B-Kommunikation, in der Unternehmen häufig sehr spezifische Zielgruppen ansprechen, eröffnet dieser Ansatz interessante Möglichkeiten.

Digitale Zwillinge ersetzen dabei nicht automatisch die klassische Marktforschung. Sie können jedoch zusätzliche Perspektiven liefern und datenbasierte Entscheidungen unterstützen, sofern die zugrunde liegenden Modelle ausreichend valide sind.

„Mit digitalen Zwillingen stehen wir vor einem spannenden Entwicklungsschritt in der Markt- und Meinungsforschung. KI ermöglicht uns, gesellschaftliche Zielgruppen auf Basis umfangreicher Datenbestände zu simulieren und damit neue Perspektiven für datenbasierte Entscheidungen zu eröffnen. Genau diese Innovationskraft wollten wir beim 4. PR Tech Day sichtbar machen, der einmal mehr bestätigt hat, dass sich die Kommunikationsbranche in einer Phase tiefgreifender Veränderung befindet. Diese Entwicklung wollen wir mit »OBSERVER« aktiv mitgestalten.“

— Florian Laszlo, »OBSERVER«

KI und Social Media: Zwischen Automatisierung und echter Markenidentität

Wie viel Künstliche Intelligenz verträgt erfolgreiche Social-Media-Kommunikation? Und welche Rolle spielt Social Media künftig im B2B-Marketing?

Diesen Fragen widmeten sich zwei weitere Programmpunkte des PR Tech Day.

Jacqueline Althaller, Geschäftsführerin von ALTHALLER Communication, präsentierte aktuelle Erkenntnisse aus der 16. Ausgabe der DACH-Langzeitstudie „Social Media in der B2B-Kommunikation“, die in Kooperation mit »OBSERVER« durchgeführt wird.

Die Untersuchung beschäftigt sich mit Entwicklungen, strategischen Erfolgsfaktoren und Veränderungen im Social-Media-Einsatz von B2B-Unternehmen im deutschsprachigen Raum.

Frederik Paschko, Director Consumer Goods & Sport bei LOBECO, beleuchtete anschließend das Spannungsfeld zwischen KI-gestützter Content-Produktion und authentischer Markenkommunikation.

Denn KI kann zwar dabei helfen, schneller mehr Inhalte zu erstellen. Eine höhere Veröffentlichungsfrequenz bedeutet jedoch nicht automatisch mehr Reichweite, Engagement oder Markenbindung.

Erfolgreiche Social-Media-Kommunikation braucht weiterhin relevante Inhalte, eine klare Markenidentität und Geschichten, die Menschen tatsächlich erreichen.

Für Social-Media-Manager:innen ergibt sich daraus eine wichtige Erkenntnis: Nicht die Menge KI-generierter Inhalte entscheidet über den Erfolg, sondern deren Qualität, Relevanz und Glaubwürdigkeit.

EU AI Act: Was KI-Regulierung für die Kommunikationsbranche bedeutet

Neben den technologischen Chancen beschäftigte sich der PR Tech Day auch mit den rechtlichen Rahmenbedingungen für den Einsatz Künstlicher Intelligenz.

Jan Lohrengel, CEO von HASTINGS AUDIO NETWORK, beleuchtete die Kennzeichnungs- und Transparenzanforderungen für KI-generierte Audioinhalte.

Im Mittelpunkt standen die Auswirkungen des europäischen AI Acts auf die Werbe- und Audiobranche sowie die Frage, welche Anforderungen Unternehmen bei der Produktion und Veröffentlichung KI-gestützter Inhalte beachten müssen.

Gerade für Kommunikationsverantwortliche, die mit synthetischen Stimmen, KI-generierten Audioformaten oder automatisierten Werbeinhalten arbeiten, gewinnt die rechtliche Einordnung an Bedeutung.

Dabei gilt: Nicht jeder KI-generierte Inhalt unterliegt denselben Kennzeichnungspflichten. Entscheidend sind unter anderem die konkrete Anwendung, die Art des Inhalts und die jeweils geltenden gesetzlichen Bestimmungen.

Für Unternehmen wird es deshalb zunehmend wichtig, technologische Innovation mit rechtlicher Sicherheit und transparenten Kommunikationsprozessen zu verbinden.

Wie KI und GEO die Rolle der PR-Beratung verändern

Auch für PR-Agenturen verändert Künstliche Intelligenz die Spielregeln. Anett Wittmann, Senior Partner bei FINN Partners, zeigte auf, wie sich die professionelle PR-Beratung in einer zunehmend KI-geprägten Kommunikationslandschaft weiterentwickelt.

Wenn KI-Systeme Informationen zusammenfassen, Quellen auswählen und Antworten auf Nutzerfragen generieren, entstehen neue Anforderungen an die strategische Positionierung von Unternehmen.

Klassische Medienarbeit bleibt relevant, wird jedoch durch zusätzliche Aufgaben ergänzt. Dazu zählen insbesondere die Optimierung von Inhalten für generative Suchsysteme, die Analyse der KI-Sichtbarkeit und die Integration KI-gestützter Workflows in bestehende Kommunikationsstrategien.

Damit erweitert sich auch das Kompetenzprofil moderner PR-Beratung. Neben journalistischem Verständnis, Medienkontakten und kreativer Kommunikationsarbeit werden technologisches Know-how, Datenkompetenz und ein fundiertes Verständnis generativer KI-Systeme immer wichtiger.

Gleichzeitig bleibt eines unverändert: Erfolgreiche PR benötigt strategisches Denken, kritische Einordnung und menschliche Kreativität.

Der perfekte KI-Workflow: Wie gelingt die Integration in den PR-Alltag?

Den Abschluss des 4. PR Tech Day bildete die Paneldiskussion „Auf der Suche nach dem perfekten KI-Workflow“.

Im Mittelpunkt stand eine Herausforderung, die derzeit zahlreiche Kommunikationsabteilungen und PR-Agenturen beschäftigt: Wie lässt sich KI sinnvoll in bestehende Arbeitsprozesse integrieren, ohne Kontrolle, Qualität und Glaubwürdigkeit zu verlieren?

Die Vorträge und Diskussionen des Nachmittags zeigten, dass erfolgreiche KI-Integration weit über die Auswahl einzelner Tools hinausgeht.

Entscheidend ist ein strategischer Ansatz, der technologische Möglichkeiten mit konkreten Kommunikationszielen verbindet.

Für die Praxis lassen sich daraus fünf zentrale Handlungsfelder ableiten:

  • KI-Sichtbarkeit analysieren: Prüfe mit Prompt Monitoring, wie deine Marke in generativen KI-Systemen dargestellt wird.
  • GEO in die Kommunikationsstrategie integrieren: Gestalte relevante, verständliche und vertrauenswürdige Inhalte, die auch von KI-Systemen als Informationsgrundlage herangezogen werden können.
  • KI-Workflows gezielt entwickeln: Identifiziere Aufgaben, bei denen KI dein Team sinnvoll unterstützt – von der Recherche bis zur Content-Erstellung.
  • Qualität und Transparenz sicherstellen: Definiere klare Verantwortlichkeiten und überprüfe KI-generierte Inhalte vor der Veröffentlichung.
  • Neue Technologien erproben: Beschäftige dich frühzeitig mit innovativen Anwendungen wie digitalen Zwillingen und KI-gestützter Zielgruppenanalyse.

Der wichtigste Erfolgsfaktor bleibt dabei die Verbindung von technologischer Effizienz und menschlicher Expertise.

Fazit: Der 4. PR Tech Day zeigt, wohin sich die Unternehmenskommunikation entwickelt

Mit seiner vierten Ausgabe bestätigte der PR Tech Day von »OBSERVER« und den CommClubs Bayern seine Bedeutung als Plattform für Innovation, Wissenstransfer und fachlichen Austausch in der Kommunikationsbranche.

Die Expert:innen von Microsoft, Edelman, FINN Partners, LOBECO, PER Connect und weiteren Unternehmen machten deutlich, wie vielfältig die Einsatzmöglichkeiten Künstlicher Intelligenz bereits heute sind.

Von Generative Engine Optimization und Prompt Monitoring über digitale Zwillinge bis hin zu KI-gestützter Content-Produktion und vertrauenswürdiger Kommunikation: Die digitale Transformation eröffnet PR- und Marketingverantwortlichen zahlreiche neue Möglichkeiten.

Gleichzeitig zeigte die Veranstaltung, dass Technologie allein keine erfolgreiche Kommunikationsstrategie ersetzt. Die Zukunft der PR liegt im intelligenten Zusammenspiel von KI, Daten, strategischer Kompetenz und menschlicher Glaubwürdigkeit.

Für Unternehmen bedeutet das, neue Entwicklungen frühzeitig zu verstehen, ihre eigene KI-Sichtbarkeit systematisch zu beobachten und innovative Technologien verantwortungsvoll einzusetzen.

Denn wer künftig nicht nur in klassischen Medien und Suchmaschinen, sondern auch in den Antworten generativer KI-Systeme präsent sein möchte, muss seine Kommunikationsstrategie entsprechend weiterentwickeln.

Der 4. PR Tech Day in Nürnberg lieferte dafür wertvolle Impulse und zeigte einmal mehr: Die Zukunft der Unternehmenskommunikation hat längst begonnen.

HIER geht es zur Bildergalerie.

Een modern thuiskantoor is tegenwoordig veel meer dan alleen een bureau en een stoel in de hoek van de kamer. Nu steeds meer mensen hybride werken of volledig vanuit huis hun taken uitvoeren, is de behoefte aan een stabiele en efficiënte digitale werkomgeving gegroeid. Een goed ingerichte werkplek draagt niet alleen bij aan de productiviteit, maar ook aan het algemene welzijn en een gezonde balans tussen werk en privé. Het begint allemaal bij de basis: een computer die doet wat hij moet doen, zonder haperingen of beveiligingsrisico's.

Bij het inrichten van een digitale werkplek kijken we vaak eerst naar de hardware, zoals een snelle laptop of een groot beeldscherm. Echter, de software die op deze apparaten draait is minstens zo belangrijk voor de dagelijkse workflow. Een up-to-date besturingssysteem zorgt ervoor dat moderne applicaties soepel draaien en dat je gegevens goed beschermd zijn tegen externe dreigingen. Voor veel gebruikers die de overstap maken naar een nieuw systeem, is een windows 11 pro download kopen een logische stap om toegang te krijgen tot geavanceerde functies zoals BitLocker-versleuteling en verbeterde integratie met zakelijke netwerken.

De impact van een opgeruimde digitale omgeving

Een rommelig bureaublad kan net zo afleidend werken als een fysiek bureau vol losse papieren. De manier waarop we onze digitale bestanden organiseren en hoe we navigeren door onze programma's heeft een directe invloed op onze mentale focus. Moderne besturingssystemen bieden tegenwoordig slimme functies om vensters te ordenen, zoals snap-lay-outs. Hiermee kun je met één klik meerdere vensters naast elkaar plaatsen, wat ideaal is voor multitasking tijdens het schrijven van rapporten of het analyseren van data.

Naast de visuele orde is de snelheid van het systeem cruciaal. Niets is frustrerender dan een computer die traag opstart op het moment dat je aan een belangrijke vergadering moet beginnen. Door te investeren in legitieme software voorkom je dat je systeem wordt vertraagd door onnodige achtergrondprocessen of verouderde stuurprogramma's. Voor gezinnen die een gedeelde computer gebruiken voor zowel schoolwerk als lichte administratie, kan een windows 11 home licentie kopen een uitstekende oplossing zijn om een veilige en gebruiksvriendelijke omgeving te creëren voor alle gezinsleden.

Balans tussen functionaliteit en esthetiek

Een lifestyle-gerichte benadering van het thuiskantoor betekent dat de techniek moet blenden met het interieur. We zien steeds vaker dat computeropstellingen worden gekozen op basis van design. Slanke monitoren, draadloze toetsenborden en een minimalistische interface dragen bij aan een rustige uitstraling van de kamer. De interface van je besturingssysteem speelt hierin ook een rol; zachte hoeken, rustige kleuren en een gecentreerde taakbalk zorgen voor een moderne 'look and feel' die minder stressvol oogt dan de drukke interfaces van vroeger.

Het personaliseren van je werkomgeving stopt niet bij het fysieke aspect. Het instellen van focus-sessies, waarbij meldingen tijdelijk worden uitgeschakeld, helpt om in een 'flow' te komen. Dit soort softwarematige hulpmiddelen zijn essentieel in een tijd waarin we constant worden bestookt met prikkels. Door je systeem zo in te richten dat het jouw natuurlijke werkritme ondersteunt, creëer je een duurzame werkplek waar je met plezier tijd doorbrengt, in plaats van een plek waar je alleen maar 'moet' zijn.

Veiligheid en privacy in de moderne lifestyle

In een wereld waar we steeds meer persoonlijke en zakelijke informatie online delen, is digitale veiligheid een integraal onderdeel van onze lifestyle geworden. We bankieren online, doen onze boodschappen via apps en bewaren dierbare foto's in de cloud. Een betrouwbaar fundament onder deze activiteiten is onmisbaar. Regelmatige updates en ingebouwde beveiligingsfuncties zorgen ervoor dat je met een gerust hart gebruik kunt maken van alle digitale gemakken die het moderne leven te bieden heeft.

Het beschermen van je privacy begint bij de keuzes die je maakt aan het begin van de installatie van je apparatuur. Door gebruik te maken van officiële licenties ben je verzekerd van de laatste beveiligingspatches en ondersteuning van de fabrikant. Dit verkleint de kans op malware en datalekken aanzienlijk. Het integreren van slimme beveiliging, zoals biometrisch inloggen met je gezicht of vingerafdruk, maakt het dagelijks gebruik niet alleen veiliger, maar ook een stuk eenvoudiger en sneller, wat perfect past bij een moderne, efficiënte levensstijl.

Παίξε

Αποτελεσματικές λύσεις για επιχειρήσεις με την atefia και προηγμένες δυνατότητες

Στον σημερινό ταχύτατα εξελισσόμενο επιχειρηματικό κόσμο, η αποτελεσματική διαχείριση και η βελτιστοποίηση των διαδικασιών είναι κρίσιμες για την επιτυχία. Η ανάγκη για λογισμικό και λύσεις που μπορούν να αυτοματοποιήσουν εργασίες, να βελτιώσουν τη συνεργασία και να παρέχουν πολύτιμες πληροφορίες έχει αυξηθεί κατακόρυφα. Η atefia, ως μια ολοκληρωμένη πλατφόρμα, προσφέρει μια σειρά από εργαλεία και δυνατότητες για να βοηθήσει τις επιχειρήσεις να αντιμετωπίσουν αυτές τις προκλήσεις και να επιτύχουν τους στόχους τους. Η ικανότητά της να προσαρμόζεται σε διαφορετικές ανάγκες και η ευκολία χρήσης της την καθιστούν μια ελκυστική επιλογή για επιχειρήσεις κάθε μεγέθους.

Η επιλογή της σωστής τεχνολογίας είναι ζωτικής σημασίας για την ανταγωνιστικότητα μιας επιχείρησης. Optimización de la Cadena de Suministro con ATEFIA

Una de las áreas donde atefia demuestra su mayor potencial es la optimización de la cadena de suministro. La gestión eficiente de materiales, componentes y productos terminados es esencial para reducir costos, minimizar retrasos y garantizar la satisfacción del cliente. ATEFIA ofrece una plataforma centralizada que permite a las empresas rastrear y controlar cada etapa de la cadena de suministro, desde la adquisición de materias primas hasta la entrega del producto final al cliente. Esto proporciona una visibilidad completa y en tiempo real de los flujos de materiales, lo que facilita la identificación de cuellos de botella y la toma de decisiones informadas para optimizar el proceso. La integración con sistemas ERP y CRM existentes es un punto fuerte.

Implementación de Sistemas de Trazabilidad

La trazabilidad de los productos es un requisito cada vez más importante en muchas industrias, especialmente en sectores como el alimentario, farmacéutico y automotriz. ATEFIA permite implementar sistemas de trazabilidad completos que registran cada movimiento de un producto a lo largo de la cadena de suministro, desde su origen hasta su destino final. Esta información es crucial para garantizar la seguridad del producto, cumplir con las regulaciones gubernamentales y responder de manera efectiva a posibles problemas de calidad. Además, la trazabilidad permite a las empresas identificar rápidamente la fuente de un problema y tomar medidas correctivas para evitar que se repita. Gestión de Activos y Mantenimiento Predictivo

Otro aspecto clave de la industria es la gestión eficiente de los activos y el mantenimiento de los equipos. ATEFIA ofrece soluciones para el seguimiento y control de los activos, permitiendo a las empresas conocer su ubicación, estado y rendimiento en tiempo real. Esto facilita la planificación del mantenimiento preventivo y predictivo, reduciendo el riesgo de averías y minimizando los tiempos de inactividad. El mantenimiento predictivo, en particular, se basa en el análisis de datos y el uso de algoritmos de aprendizaje automático para predecir cuándo es probable que falle un equipo, permitiendo a las empresas programar el mantenimiento antes de que ocurra la avería. Esto reduce significativamente los costos y mejora la disponibilidad de los activos.

El Rol de los Sensores IoT

Los sensores de Internet de las Cosas (IoT) desempeñan un papel fundamental en la gestión de activos y el mantenimiento predictivo con atefia. Estos sensores recopilan datos en tiempo real sobre el estado de los equipos, como la temperatura, la vibración, la presión y el consumo de energía. Estos datos se envían a la plataforma atefia, donde se analizan para identificar patrones y tendencias que puedan indicar un problema inminente. La integración de sensores IoT permite a las empresas pasar de un mantenimiento reactivo a un mantenimiento proactivo, optimizando la vida útil de los activos y reduciendo los costos de mantenimiento. La seguridad de los datos recopilados por los sensores IoT es una consideración importante.

  • Monitorización continua del estado de los activos.

  • Optimización de los programas de mantenimiento.
  • Reducción de los tiempos de inactividad.

La capacidad de atefia para integrarse con sistemas de gestión de mantenimiento computarizado (CMMS) permite a las empresas automatizar los flujos de trabajo de mantenimiento y mejorar la eficiencia de sus equipos de mantenimiento. La generación de informes detallados sobre el rendimiento de los activos proporciona información valiosa para la toma de decisiones estratégicas.

El control de calidad es un aspecto crítico en cualquier proceso industrial, y atefia ofrece herramientas para garantizar que los productos cumplen con los estándares de calidad requeridos. La plataforma permite registrar y analizar datos de calidad en cada etapa de la producción, identificar las causas de los defectos y tomar medidas correctivas para mejorar el proceso. Además, atefia ayuda a las empresas a cumplir con las regulaciones gubernamentales y los estándares de la industria, proporcionando una documentación completa y auditable de los procesos de control de calidad. Automatización de Inspecciones

La automatización de las inspecciones de calidad mediante el uso de visión artificial y otras tecnologías avanzadas permite a las empresas detectar defectos de manera más rápida y precisa. ATEFIA se integra con sistemas de visión artificial que pueden inspeccionar productos en tiempo real y detectar defectos que serían difíciles de identificar manualmente. Esto reduce el riesgo de que productos defectuosos lleguen al cliente y mejora la reputación de la empresa. La capacidad de atefia para registrar y analizar datos de calidad permite a las empresas identificar las causas raíz de los defectos y tomar medidas correctivas para mejorar el proceso de producción. La integración de atefia con sistemas de automatización industrial, como PLCs, SCADA y robots, permite a las empresas crear fábricas inteligentes y optimizar sus procesos de producción. Por ejemplo, atefia puede utilizar datos de un PLC para ajustar la velocidad de una línea de producción o para programar el mantenimiento de un robot. El futuro de la industria está intrínsecamente ligado a la Industria 4.0, un concepto que engloba la digitalización, la automatización y la interconexión de los procesos industriales. ATEFIA está preparada para desempeñar un papel crucial en esta transformación, proporcionando la plataforma y las herramientas necesarias para que las empresas aprovechen al máximo las oportunidades que ofrece la Industria 4.0. How to Navigate Time-Sensitive Market Sections

📅 Sep 20, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Navigating fast-paced financial environments requires a well-defined approach, sharp focus, and the ability to interpret rapid developments without hesitation. When trading or investing within time-sensitive market sections, traditional long-term indicators often take a backseat to immediate momentum signals and volatile order flow. Market participants must quickly evaluate changing liquidity conditions, sudden price spikes, and dynamic bid-ask spreads. Successfully operating in these short windows demands structured preparation before the opening bell rings. Without an established framework, reacting to abrupt swings can lead to costly missteps, heightened stress, and emotional decision-making that disrupts your overall trading plan and jeopardizes your available capital.

To manage high-frequency fluctuations effectively, traders should establish clear entry parameters, target price levels, and predefined exit thresholds prior to entering any active position. Technical setups such as breakout points, moving average crossovers, and volume spikes serve as reliable triggers in rapid sessions. Because prices can shift in fractions of a second, relying solely on intuition is rarely sustainable over extended periods. Implementing structured routines allows you to execute orders systematically, filtering out market noise while focusing strictly on high-probability setups available during key volatility periods across diverse, competitive market environments and challenging trading conditions that require immediate tactical clarity.

In addition to technical charting tools, staying connected with real-time sentiment streams can offer a crucial informational advantage. Observing how retail and institutional sentiment evolves provides valuable context around sudden momentum shifts. Modern digital platforms and interactive networks, including dynamic spaces like LLWIN SOCIAL, enable active participants to observe collective trends, exchange analytical perspectives, and evaluate overarching sentiment shifts in real time. Combining these collaborative insights with disciplined charting strategies creates a comprehensive view of the landscape, helping traders anticipate volume surges rather than merely reacting after the move has already occurred across active and highly liquid modern trading exchanges.

Managing risk exposure is arguably the most critical component when dealing with compressed timeframes. Because market volatility increases significantly during scheduled economic releases or corporate earnings announcements, position sizing must be carefully adjusted downward to account for wider price swings. Utilizing automated stop-loss orders and trailing profit targets ensures that capital remains protected even if an unexpected price reversal takes place. Experienced market operators never risk an excessive portion of their overall portfolio on a single fleeting opportunity, understanding that longevity in trading depends entirely on proactive capital preservation, strict discipline, and systematic risk mitigation across every single executed order.

Finally, maintaining psychological discipline prevents the destructive urge to chase market trades that have already extended beyond optimal risk-reward ratios. Missing a sudden market breakout is far better than entering late at an unfavorable price level. After completing a session, conducting a detailed post-trade review helps identify procedural strengths and recurring execution weaknesses. Tracking execution speed, slippage, and emotional triggers builds long-term consistency. By combining proactive planning, continuous data analysis, strict risk controls, and mental resilience, any committed trader can confidently navigate time-sensitive market sections and secure sustainable results across changing market conditions over the course of their trading journey.

How to Understand Selections on a Bet Slip

📅 Sep 19, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Navigating an online wagering interface can initially seem daunting, but mastering the fundamentals of your digital bet slip is the single most essential step toward making informed gaming decisions. When you browse through diverse sports fixtures or competitive tournament markets, clicking on a predicted outcome immediately transfers that specific pick onto your active electronic ticket. Each entry displayed represents an individual selection, highlighting vital operational details such as the event name, the designated market category, and the prevailing odds. Platforms like LLwin present these dynamic choices clearly so bettors can effortlessly review prospective wagers before committing any real funds to their tickets. Developing a solid comprehension of how these distinct components interact allows you to manage personal risk effectively while maintaining complete strategic control over your overall wagering budget without unexpected confusion.

The primary and foundational element of any bet slip is the specific market you have selected. This might range from straightforward moneyline picks, where you simply choose an outright winner, to more intricate point spreads, handicap margins, or over and under statistical totals. Next to each event title, you will observe the active odds format, which generally appears as decimal, fractional, or American values depending on your preferred interface settings. Decimal odds reflect your complete return including your original stake, whereas fractional odds indicate prospective profit relative to your wager. Scrutinizing these numerical values ensures you accurately recognize the implied probability of an outcome occurring, enabling you to identify genuine market value across all active events rather than making impulsive, uninformed wagers based on superficial intuition alone.

Another essential aspect involves distinguishing between single wagers and multi-selection combination bets, frequently referred to as accumulators or parlays. If you place several independent choices onto your slip, the software system typically enables you to treat them as separate single bets or combine them into one unified wager. In a combined accumulator, the mathematical odds of every individual selection multiply together, producing a substantially higher potential return from a relatively modest initial investment. However, every single prediction on that ticket must prove correct for the final payout to be awarded; just one incorrect result invalidates the entire combination. Evaluating this inherent risk dynamic helps you determine whether combining events properly aligns with your personal risk tolerance and strategic goals.

Finally, you must pay strict attention to the stake field and potential payout calculation before clicking the confirmation button. The stake is the exact financial sum you choose to allocate to a wager, and entering an amount automatically calculates the total gross return. Reputable gaming portals also display relevant settlement rules, active cash-out features, and maximum win thresholds directly adjacent to your ticket layout for complete transparency. Always review every entry on your slip carefully to verify that you have not accidentally selected the wrong team or reversed a handicap prior to final submission. Maintaining consistent, patient attention to these fundamental mechanics ensures a disciplined, responsible, and structured approach toward every betting opportunity you pursue online over time, taking critical factors into account.

Die Planung und Durchführung von Veranstaltungen hat sich in den letzten Jahren grundlegend gewandelt. Wo früher dicke Aktenordner, unzählige Excel-Tabellen und handschriftliche Notizen den Alltag in Event-Locations prägten, setzen heute immer mehr Betreiber auf digitale Lösungen. Die Erwartungshaltung der Kunden ist gestiegen: Schnelligkeit, Professionalität und eine reibungslose Kommunikation werden vorausgesetzt. Wer hier noch manuell arbeitet, verliert schnell den Anschluss an den Wettbewerb und riskiert Fehler in der Buchungslogistik.

Die Digitalisierung bietet jedoch weit mehr als nur die bloße Ablösung von Papier. Es geht darum, komplexe Prozesse zu vereinfachen und Transparenz für das gesamte Team zu schaffen. Wenn alle Beteiligten – vom Vertrieb über das Catering bis hin zur Technik – in Echtzeit auf denselben Informationsstand zugreifen können, sinkt die Fehlerquote gegen Null. Dies ist die Grundlage für ein erstklassiges Gästeerlebnis und eine effiziente Auslastung der Räumlichkeiten.

Effizienzsteigerung durch spezialisierte IT-Lösungen

Für Betreiber von Veranstaltungszentren, Hotels mit Tagungsräumen oder besonderen Off-Locations ist die Wahl der richtigen IT-Infrastruktur entscheidend. Eine professionelle Management Software für Event Locations ermöglicht es, Anfragen zentral zu verwalten, Angebote innerhalb von Minuten zu erstellen und die Verfügbarkeit von Ressourcen sofort zu prüfen. Statt Zeit mit administrativen Routineaufgaben zu verschwenden, können sich die Mitarbeiter wieder auf das Wesentliche konzentrieren: die Beratung des Kunden und die kreative Ausgestaltung der Events.

Ein weiterer entscheidender Vorteil ist die Automatisierung von Schnittstellen. Moderne Systeme lassen sich nahtlos in bestehende Webseiten integrieren, sodass Kunden direkt online Anfragen stellen können, die sofort im Backoffice landen. Das spart nicht nur Zeit, sondern erhöht auch die Conversion-Rate, da die Reaktionszeit auf Kundenanfragen drastisch verkürzt wird. In einer Branche, in der der Erste oft den Zuschlag erhält, ist dies ein unschätzbarer Marktvorteil.

Die Rolle von Daten und Analysen im Eventmanagement

Neben der reinen Organisation spielt die Datenauswertung eine immer wichtigere Rolle. Durch die zentrale Erfassung aller Buchungsvorgänge entstehen wertvolle Datenpools. Betreiber können genau analysieren, welche Zeiträume besonders gefragt sind, welche Pakete die höchsten Margen erzielen und wo eventuelle Engpässe in der Ressourcenplanung liegen. Diese Erkenntnisse sind die Basis für fundierte unternehmerische Entscheidungen und eine langfristige Wachstumsstrategie.

Um diese Potenziale voll auszuschöpfen, bedarf es einer intuitiven Benutzeroberfläche, die von allen Teammitgliedern ohne langwierige Schulungen bedient werden kann. Die Tools von MICE Operations zeigen hierbei eindrucksvoll, wie Komplexität reduziert werden kann, ohne an Funktionstiefe einzubüßen. Die Cloud-basierte Architektur sorgt zudem dafür, dass der Zugriff ortsunabhängig möglich ist – ein Muss in der heutigen mobilen Arbeitswelt.

Nachhaltigkeit und Zukunftsfähigkeit in der Branche

Ein oft unterschätzter Aspekt der Digitalisierung ist der Beitrag zur Nachhaltigkeit. Durch den Verzicht auf papierbasierte Prozesse und die Optimierung der Logistik können Ressourcen geschont werden. Digitale Raumpläne und Catering-Listen reduzieren den Verschnitt und sorgen für eine präzisere Planung. Dies spart nicht nur Kosten, sondern zahlt auch auf das grüne Image einer Location ein, was für viele Firmenkunden mittlerweile ein hartes Auswahlkriterium bei der Buchung darstellt.

Die technologische Entwicklung steht nicht still. Künstliche Intelligenz wird in Zukunft dabei helfen, Buchungstrends noch genauer vorherzusagen oder die Kommunikation mit Kunden über intelligente Chatbots weiter zu automatisieren. Wer heute die Basis mit einer soliden digitalen Struktur legt, ist für diese kommenden Innovationen bestens gerüstet. Es geht darum, eine flexible Umgebung zu schaffen, die mit den Anforderungen der Kunden und den Möglichkeiten der Technik mitwächst. Zo können Veranstaltungsorte ihre Resilienz stärken und auch in dynamischen Marktphasen erfolgreich agieren.
